content.text:
Apple’s -7.16% rolling move from February 11 to February 13 looks like one coherent selloff rather than a reversal: AAPL was at a $275.50 prior close before a roughly 5% drop on February 12, then continued lower on February 13 from a $261.73 prior close to about $255.78, down another 2.3% [1][2]. The dominant catalyst was firm-specific: after the February 11 close, Bloomberg reported that Apple’s long-planned Siri upgrade had hit internal-testing snags and that features expected for iOS 26.4 could slip into later releases such as iOS 26.5 or iOS 27 [3]. That directly challenged the Apple Intelligence/Siri product-timing narrative; Evercore ISI reportedly expected Apple Intelligence 2.0 to be delayed from March, even while keeping an Outperform rating and $330 target [4].

A second Apple-specific overhang arrived on February 12, when the FTC announced that Chairman Andrew Ferguson had sent Tim Cook a warning letter tied to Apple News curation, saying viewpoint-based promotion or suppression could violate the FTC Act if inconsistent with Apple’s terms or consumer expectations [5]. That regulatory headline was probably not large enough by itself to explain a 7% two-day drop, but it added to a cluster of Apple-specific concerns; MarketBeat’s February 13 recap explicitly tied the Friday follow-through to sector rotation, AI fears, a Siri delay, and the FTC letter [2]. This aligns with the attribution showing most of the episode as firm-specific.

The industry and market pieces were also real, not just background noise. On February 12, U.S. stocks fell sharply as investors punished companies seen as AI losers; the S&P 500 lost 1.6% and the Nasdaq fell 2.0%, with AP noting AI-disruption worries and pre-CPI rate volatility [6]. Nasdaq later described the broader technology pullback as an “AI scare trade,” with institutional selling and AI-disruption fears spilling across sectors [7]. Macro pressure eased on February 13 after softer inflation data helped steady the market, with the S&P 500 nearly flat and the Nasdaq down only 0.2%; AAPL’s continued -2.3% decline that day therefore looks more Apple/tech-positioning driven than a pure market move [8][2]. Evidence is strongest for the February 12 catalyst cluster and somewhat thinner for the February 13 continuation, but the dated sources support a composite selloff led by Apple-specific AI-delay and regulatory headlines, amplified by a broader tech/AI-risk rotation.
